To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cognitive impairment with age is associated with changes in the proteome of the hippocampus.

cognitive impairment is associated with changes in the expression of proteins that are involved in the glycolysis pathway, the ubiquitination pathway, and the proteasome pathway, and that behavioral stratification is important for the detection of these changes.

cognitive impairment is associated with age-dependent changes in the hippocampus, and that proteomic analysis of behaviorally defined animals reveals changes that would not be evident in the absence of behavioral stratification.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying cognitive aging and age-related cognitive decline.
the identification of the molecular mechanisms underlying age-related cognitive decline.
the identification and characterization of molecular mechanisms that underlie cognitive decline in aging.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the proteomic changes are associated with cognitive decline and are not the result of aging per se, but rather the result of the synergistic effects of aging and other perturbations.
aging is associated with changes in the hippocampus proteome and that these changes are associated with cognitive impairment, but not necessarily with aging per se.
the proteome of the hippocampus is highly dynamic and changes dramatically with age.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
age-related changes in hippocampal proteomics are associated with cognitive decline.
age-related changes in cognitive performance are associated with changes in protein expression, and that the proteome is a complex and dynamic entity that is altered by age and cognitive performance.

age-related alterations in protein expression are not the sole cause of cognitive decline, but act synergistically with perturbations such as inflammation, oxidative stress, and mitochondrial dysfunction to result in cognitive impairment.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the proteomic changes we have observed are not the sole cause of the cognitive decline observed in aged rats, but rather are likely a result of the underlying age-related changes in dendritic and synaptodendritic morphology.
the proteome is a dynamic system that changes with age and that cognitive performance is a major factor influencing the age-related proteomic changes.
age-related changes in hippocampal protein expression are not necessarily associated with cognitive impairment.
